verses.text: Some men came down from Judea and taught the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised after the custom of Moses, you can’t be saved.”

Therefore when Paul and Barnabas had no small discord and discussion with them, they appointed Paul and Barnabas, and some others of them, to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question.
They, being sent on their way by the assembly, passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, declaring the conversion of the Gentiles. They caused great joy to all the brothers.
When they had come to Jerusalem, they were received by the assembly and the apostles and the elders, and they reported all things that God had done with them.
But some of the sect of the Pharisees who believed rose up, saying, “It is necessary to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses.”
The apostles and the elders were gathered together to see about this matter.

When there had been much discussion, Peter rose up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that a good while ago God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the nations should hear the word of the Good News, and believe.
God, who knows the heart, testified about them, giving them the Holy Spirit, just like he did to us.
He made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith.
Now therefore why do you tempt God, that you should put a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?
But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus,  just as they are.”
All the multitude kept silence, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul reporting what signs and wonders God had done among the nations through them.
After they were silent, James answered, “Brothers, listen to me.
Simeon has reported how God first visited the nations, to take out of them a people for his name.
This agrees with the words of the prophets. As it is written,
‘After these things I will return. I will again build the tabernacle of David, which has fallen. I will again build its ruins. I will set it up,
That the rest of men may seek after the Lord; all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who does all these things.
All of God’s works are known to him from eternity.’
“Therefore my judgment is that we don’t trouble those from among the Gentiles who turn to God,
but that we write to them that they abstain from the pollution of idols, from sexual immorality, from what is strangled, and from blood.
For Moses from generations of old has in every city those who preach him, being read in the synagogues every Sabbath.”

Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole assembly, to choose men out of their company, and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, chief men among the brothers.
They wrote these things by their hand: “The apostles, the elders, and the brothers, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: greetings.
Because we have heard that some who went out from us have troubled you with words, unsettling your souls, saying, ‘You must be circumcised and keep the law,’ to whom we gave no commandment;
it seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose out men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
We have sent therefore Judas and Silas, who themselves will also tell you the same things by word of mouth.
For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things:
that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality, from which if you keep yourselves, it will be well with you. Farewell.”
So, when they were sent off, they came to Antioch. Having gathered the multitude together, they delivered the letter.
When they had read it, they rejoiced over the encouragement.
Judas and Silas, also being prophets themselves, encouraged the brothers with many words, and strengthened them.
After they had spent some time there, they were sent back with greetings from the brothers to the apostles.
None
But Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.
After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.”
Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also.
But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work.
Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him, and sailed away to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas, and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God.
He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.

footnotes.content: A question reaches from Judea that will shape the whole church: must we keep Moses before we follow Jesus? These men speak with authority, but they don't yet see that grace has already broken past every border.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul and Barnabas don't back down or dismiss the question—they meet it head-on. When the assembly decides to send them to Jerusalem, you see what the body of Christ does when it's anxious: it doesn't fragment, it gathers to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As the company travels through Phoenicia and Samaria, they declare what God has done with the Gentiles—and the believers there rejoice. Joy is the sign that truth is traveling. These are places once thought 'outside'—now the joy spreads through them too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jerusalem receives them, and Paul and Barnabas rehearse everything God did. Notice: they lead with God's work, not their argument. When you're uncertain, letting what the Lord has *already done* speak first takes the pressure off your words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even among believers—even among those who came to faith through the law—some cannot yet let it go as a gateway for others. Belief in Jesus doesn't always immediately untangle us from what once held us safe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The apostles and elders gather. It's a council, deliberate and careful, not a hasty vote. Sometimes the bravest thing faith does is stop and ask hard questions together before deciding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter stands—the same Peter who once couldn't eat with Gentiles, now testifying that God showed *him* first, years ago, that salvation comes by the Good News alone. His own journey becomes his authority to speak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God looks at the heart and sees what matters: faith. The Holy Spirit came to Gentiles the same way—no ceremony, no law-keeping first, just belief. When the Spirit moves, He settles the question.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No distinction. In one short verse, Peter says what took decades to sink into the early church: grace doesn't grade people. A Gentile heart made clean by faith is as clean as a Jewish heart made clean by faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Why tempt God? That's the sharp question—to demand the law from others would be to test whether God's grace is truly enough. It's wise, pointed, and kind all at once.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter closes with the anchor: *all of us*, Jew and Gentile alike, stand on the same ground—the grace of the Lord Jesus. Not our background, not our works, not our history. Only grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The room falls silent—a sign that hearts are listening, not defending. Then Barnabas and Paul speak, and the proof they offer is the simplest: signs and wonders God has done. The work itself witnesses.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After the silence, James speaks—the Lord's brother, leader of Jerusalem. His few words suggest he's been listening more than talking, waiting to hear what the Spirit would settle first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: James frames it simply: God visited the Gentiles to call a people for His name. It's not an exception or an afterthought—it's God's *first* work among them. He was there before we realized it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then James turns to the prophets—Amos 9:11–12—and reads it to the council. He's not using Scripture as a weapon but as a mirror, showing that this moment was written long before.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The tabernacle of David shall be rebuilt—the kingdom restored. James is saying: God promised this opening long ago. Not as penalty for failure, but as the design all along.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rest of mankind may seek the Lord—all the Gentiles *who are called by His name*. Inclusion isn't an accident; it's woven into the old promise itself. God's generosity was never a new idea.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All God's works are known to Him from eternity. Not sudden inspiration—certain, foreseen, already decided before the foundation was laid. Gentiles were always meant to come home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: James's judgment: don't trouble the Gentiles who turn to God. No ceremonies, no law-keeping gates. Just let them come. How many of us would have the courage to say that aloud?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet he offers four practical guardrails—idolatry, sexual immorality, things strangled, blood—rooted in kindness toward Jewish brothers who still found these difficult. Unity sometimes looks like meeting your neighbor halfway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses is preached in every synagogue every Sabbath—so the law isn't forgotten, just freed from being a gatekeeper. Gentile converts will learn the depths of it in time, without it blocking their entry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The decision becomes one of the whole assembly, not a council pronouncement. Judas and Silas are chosen—leaders recognized among the brothers—to carry the news. Trust travels better when it has a face and a voice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The letter they write isn't stern or condescending. It's from the apostles, elders, and *brothers*—a family saying: we heard, we listened, we decided together, here's what we're sending you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They acknowledge the trouble plainly: some went out and unsettled the churches with words we never authorized. Honesty first—we know what happened, we see the wound, and we're closing the gap.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Having come to one accord—unanimity, the Spirit's work visible in agreement—they send trusted messengers alongside Paul and Barnabas. Leadership is known by who it trusts and how it travels.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Men who have risked their lives for Jesus—Paul and Barnabas are named by their sacrifice, not their titles. In the end, what makes someone trustworthy is what they've been willing to lose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judas and Silas will confirm everything by word of mouth. The letter is backed by presence, by conversation, by the chance for questions and reassurance face-to-face. Words on a page aren't enough; you send your own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us—the simplest claim and the most profound: the Spirit and the apostles moved together. No burden laid beyond what's necessary. Mercy measured out carefully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four things to avoid for conscience's sake, and then: it will be well with you. Not law, but love. The council's last word is not judgment but peace and a promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They come to Antioch and gather the multitude. The letter must be read aloud, in assembly, so every voice hears it the same way. Transparency lived out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They rejoiced over the encouragement—the relief is palpable. A cloud of fear lifts. Someone said, 'You are welcome here, as you are.' For Gentile believers waiting in the shadows, it was everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judas and Silas, themselves prophets, speak many words of encouragement. It's not just the letter that heals—it's the people behind it, speaking alive and in real time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After they spent time strengthening, they were sent back with greetings. A small detail: they stayed, they didn't rush. Healing takes presence, not just a memo.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: None—a verse that carries no text, yet it's here. Sometimes the most honest pages are the quiet ones, the spaces where no more needs to be said.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word with many others. The council is closed, but the real work—building the church day by day—goes on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul says to Barnabas: let's go back and see how our brothers are doing. The work of an apostle isn't about staying safe—it's about returning to tend the flock you've opened.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Barnabas wanted to take John Mark. After Mark left them in Pamphylia, Barnabas didn't forget him—he believed in second chances. That's the kind of heart Barnabas had.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul disagreed—not harshly, but firmly. Mark had withdrawn before; Paul saw it as unfinished business, too risky for the work ahead. Different men see failure differently.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The contention grew sharp, and they separated. Looking back, readers today hear an echo of what happens when good people disagree deeply: even God-sent apostles can part ways. The kingdom survives the fracture, and sends the gospel *both* directions at once.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul chose Silas and was commended by the brothers to the grace of God. Even in disagreement, the church doesn't withhold blessing. Both journeys would bear fruit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies. The chapter closes where it opens—with the apostles moving forward, doing the work, trusting that God was in the council and in the road alike.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
